changes.before: Implement Tag value equality for Tag instances by text. Return NotImplemented from a direct __eq__ call with an unsupported type. Preserve identity semantics and do not claim all objects with a text attribute are Tags.
changes.after: Let two Tag objects compare equal when their text matches.

before: Two separate objects can represent the same value. Tag equality compares their text fields. The == operator can ask __eq__ for this rule; is still asks whether two names refer to the same object. Defining equality does not change identity.

__eq__(self, other) receives the other operand. isinstance(other, Tag) checks whether this rule supports it. Return the special singleton NotImplemented for an unsupported type, rather than raising NotImplementedError or pretending the type was understood. This lets Python try the other operand’s comparison behavior.

If neither operand supports equality with the other, == falls back to identity comparison. In this example a Tag and a string are distinct objects, so they compare False even if their displayed text matches. Do not treat NotImplemented as a Boolean result in your own if statement.

A custom equality rule also matters when values are compared in collections. It does not automatically make the object a safe dictionary key. The next hash-contract lesson addresses that separately; do not add an arbitrary hash just to suppress an error.

```python
class Tag:
    def __init__(self, text):
        self.text = text

    def __eq__(self, other):
        if not isinstance(other, Tag):
            return NotImplemented
        return self.text == other.text
left = Tag("music")
right = Tag("music")
print(left == right)
print(left is right)
print(left == "music")
```
Equal text prints True, separate identity prints False, and the unsupported string comparison ultimately prints False.

Implement Tag value equality for Tag instances by text. Return NotImplemented from a direct __eq__ call with an unsupported type. Preserve identity semantics and do not claim all objects with a text attribute are Tags.
after:
Two separate `Tag` objects can hold matching text. We can make `==` use `__eq__` to compare that text.

`is` still asks whether the objects are the very same one. Changing the rule for `==` does not change this identity check.

`__eq__(self, other)` receives the other value to compare. `isinstance(other, Tag)` checks whether it is a `Tag`.

For other kinds of values, return `NotImplemented`. This tells Python to try the other value's comparison rule.

`NotImplemented` is a special value to return. It is different from raising the error `NotImplementedError`.

If neither value knows how to compare with the other, `==` checks whether they are the same object.

Here, a `Tag` and a string are separate objects. They compare `False` even if their text looks the same.

Do not use `NotImplemented` as a true-or-false answer in your own `if` check.

Collections can use your `__eq__` rule when comparing their items. But adding this rule does not make your object ready to use as a dictionary key.

Dictionary keys also need a hash: a number Python uses to help find a key. The next lesson explains this. Do not add a made-up hash just to hide an error.

```python
class Tag:
    def __init__(self, text):
        self.text = text

    def __eq__(self, other):
        if not isinstance(other, Tag):
            return NotImplemented
        return self.text == other.text
left = Tag("music")
right = Tag("music")
print(left == right)
print(left is right)
print(left == "music")
```
Output:
```text
True
False
False
```
The two Tags have equal text, so the first answer is `True`. They are separate objects, so the second is `False`. Comparing this Tag with a string also gives `False`.

Build `Tag`'s equality rule. For two `Tag` objects, compare their text.

When `__eq__` receives another kind of value, return `NotImplemented`. Having a `text` attribute alone does not make an object a `Tag`.

Leave the `is` identity check unchanged.
